argument: When new nodes attach preferentially to already well-connected nodes, network degree can develop a power-law tail. Hubs then dominate connectivity, search, diffusion, and vulnerability.
boundary: Many empirical networks are not pure power laws, and multiple mechanisms produce heavy tails.
Finite size, aging, cost, and constraints modify exponents.
Degree distribution alone does not determine dynamics or causality.
claim: When new nodes attach preferentially to already well-connected nodes, network degree can develop a power-law tail. Hubs then dominate connectivity, search, diffusion, and vulnerability.
interpretation: Principia should distinguish “heavy-tailed” from “scale-free” and report fitting range and alternatives.
